Clement Howell

Biography

Introduction

Clement Ernest Howell (December 10, 1935 – August 2, 1987) is revered as one of the most dedicated public servants in the history of the Turks and Caicos Islands. Known primarily today as the namesake of the territory's largest public secondary school, his life was a testament to the power of education, civic responsibility, and steadfast leadership. In an archipelago that was historically marginalized and economically underdeveloped, Howell emerged as a beacon of progress and a champion for the empowerment of his people. His legacy is etched not only in the institution that bears his name but in the foundational political and social structures he helped build.

Early Life and Background

Born on December 10, 1935, in the settlement of Blue Hills on the island of Providenciales, Clement Howell entered a world characterized by geographic isolation and economic hardship. The Turks and Caicos Islands in the 1930s were heavily reliant on the salt industry, fishing, and subsistence agriculture. Providenciales, now the bustling tourist hub of the nation, was then a quiet, tight-knit community where everyone knew their neighbors, and survival depended on communal solidarity.

Howell was the son of Edgar Cornelius and Christiana Howell. His parents instilled in him a strong work ethic, a deep respect for education, and a profound sense of duty to his community. In an era when formal schooling was limited, the Howell family recognized that knowledge was the key to unlocking a better future. Clement's early years were shaped by the rhythms of island life—the harsh sun, the unforgiving sea, and the enduring spirit of the islanders. These formative experiences forged a man of immense resilience and unyielding determination.

"To understand the man is to understand the soil from which he sprang—a soil that demanded resilience and rewarded community."

A Champion of Education

Howell’s early career was defined by his commitment to education. Recognizing the dire need for qualified teachers in his community, he took up the mantle of an educator. He taught at the Five Cays All Age School and the Blue Hills All Age School, institutions that were the lifeblood of the local communities. In these classrooms, Howell did more than impart academic knowledge; he shaped the character of his students, teaching them the values of discipline, respect, and civic duty.

Education in the Turks and Caicos during this period was fraught with challenges. Resources were scarce, infrastructure was rudimentary, and the curriculum was often disconnected from the realities of island life. Despite these obstacles, Howell was a transformative figure in the classroom. He advocated for better facilities, updated teaching materials, and a curriculum that celebrated the islands' unique heritage while preparing students for the broader world. His tenure as a teacher left an indelible mark on generations of Turks and Caicos Islanders, many of whom would go on to assume leadership roles in their own right.

Civic Engagement and Local Leadership

Beyond the classroom, Howell was deeply involved in the civic life of Providenciales. He served as the Secretary and Chairman of the District Board for Providenciales, a crucial local government body responsible for overseeing the island's affairs. In this capacity, Howell was instrumental in advocating for infrastructure improvements, economic development initiatives, and better public services. He was a tireless advocate for his community, often traveling to the capital, Grand Turk, to lobby for resources and support.

Howell also served as a District Constable, a role that underscored his commitment to law and order and the well-being of his fellow citizens. As a constable, he was not merely an enforcer of the law but a mediator, a counselor, and a trusted community leader. His deep understanding of the local culture and his unwavering sense of justice earned him the respect and admiration of all who knew him.

Political Ascent and the Interim Advisory Council

Howell's transition from local leader to national political figure was a natural progression. He aligned himself with the People's Democratic Movement (PDM), a political party that championed the rights of the working class and advocated for greater autonomy for the Turks and Caicos Islands. His eloquence, integrity, and deep connection to the grassroots made him a formidable political force.

The mid-1980s was a period of profound political turmoil in the Turks and Caicos Islands. In 1986, following an official enquiry led by Louis Bloom-Cooper, the British Government suspended the territory's ministerial government. The enquiry had uncovered evidence of unconstitutional behavior, political discrimination, and administrative malpractice among previous ministers. It was a dark chapter in the islands' history, a time of uncertainty and disillusionment.

In the wake of this crisis, the British Government established an interim advisory council to govern the territory until democratic elections could be held. Clement Howell was appointed to this crucial body, serving from July 1986 until his untimely death in 1987. His appointment was a testament to his unblemished reputation and his proven ability to govern with wisdom and integrity.

As a member of the advisory council, Howell played a vital role in stabilizing the government and restoring public confidence. He worked tirelessly to address the systemic issues that had led to the crisis, advocating for transparency, accountability, and the rule of law. His leadership during this critical period helped lay the groundwork for the restoration of democratic governance in the Turks and Caicos Islands.

Personal Life and Tragic Passing

Howell was a devoted family man. He was married to Ellen Amelia Jolly, and together they built a home that was a sanctuary of love, faith, and mutual support. Their partnership was a source of strength for Howell, providing him with the emotional foundation he needed to navigate the challenges of public life.

Tragically, Clement Howell's life was cut short when he died on August 2, 1987, at the age of 51. His passing sent shockwaves through the Turks and Caicos Islands, plunging the nation into a state of profound mourning. The loss of such a visionary leader, particularly at a time when the territory was still navigating its way out of a political crisis, was deeply felt by all.

A Lasting Legacy

Though his life was brief, Clement Howell's legacy endures. In September 1987, just weeks after his death, the government opened the Clement Howell High School in Providenciales. Naming the institution in his honor was a fitting tribute to a man who had dedicated his life to the education and empowerment of his people.

Today, the Clement Howell High School is the largest government-operated secondary school in the Turks and Caicos Islands. It stands as a beacon of academic excellence and a testament to Howell's enduring impact. The school has produced countless leaders in politics, business, education, and the arts, all of whom carry forward Howell's vision of a prosperous, educated, and self-reliant Turks and Caicos.

Furthermore, Howell's legacy serves as a reminder of the importance of integrity, service, and sacrifice in public life. In an era marked by cynicism and political division, his life stands as a shining example of what it means to truly serve one's country. He is remembered not merely as a politician or an educator, but as a patriot who gave his all for the betterment of the Turks and Caicos Islands. His story is inextricably woven into the fabric of the nation's history, a source of inspiration for generations to come.

The political landscape of the Turks and Caicos Islands in the 1970s and 1980s was characterized by a push for modernization and an evolving relationship with the United Kingdom. The People's Democratic Movement (PDM), the party to which Howell belonged, was at the forefront of this movement. Founded by J.A.G.S. McCartney, the PDM was driven by a vision of social justice, economic self-reliance, and political autonomy. Howell's affiliation with the PDM was deeply rooted in his own experiences as an educator and community leader. He understood that true progress could only be achieved if the voices of ordinary citizens were heard and their needs addressed.

His work within the PDM was instrumental in shaping the party's platform, particularly its focus on education and social welfare. Howell believed that a nation's greatest asset was its people, and he championed policies that invested in human capital. He advocated for scholarships for promising students, vocational training programs for the youth, and better healthcare facilities for the elderly. His vision was comprehensive and inclusive, reflecting a deep understanding of the interconnectedness of social and economic development.

The 1986 constitutional crisis was a defining moment in Howell's career. The suspension of the ministerial government was a severe blow to the territory's democratic aspirations. It was a time of intense scrutiny and national soul-searching. The Bloom-Cooper commission's findings laid bare the fragility of the islands' political institutions and the urgent need for reform. In this fraught environment, Howell emerged as a voice of reason and a stabilizing force.

His service on the interim advisory council was marked by a commitment to transparency and accountability. He understood that the council's mandate was not merely to govern, but to restore the moral authority of the state. He worked closely with his colleagues to implement reforms that strengthened the civil service, improved financial management, and safeguarded against corruption. His efforts were guided by a steadfast belief in the rule of law and the inviolability of democratic principles.

Moreover, Howell's leadership during this period helped to bridge the divide between the government and the governed. He was accessible, empathetic, and always willing to listen to the concerns of his fellow citizens. He held town hall meetings, visited schools and community centers, and engaged in a continuous dialogue with the public. His approachable demeanor and his genuine concern for the welfare of the people endeared him to the nation.

In reflecting on the life and legacy of Clement Ernest Howell, one is struck by the depth of his commitment and the breadth of his impact. He was a man of many parts—an educator, a civic leader, a politician, and a patriot. But above all, he was a servant of the people. His life was a testament to the transformative power of leadership that is grounded in empathy, integrity, and a profound sense of duty.

The Turks and Caicos Islands of today is a fundamentally different place from the one Howell knew. It is a modern, thriving nation, recognized globally for its natural beauty and economic vitality. Yet, the foundations of this prosperity were laid by individuals like Clement Howell, who worked tirelessly in the shadows to build a better future for their homeland. As the students of Clement Howell High School walk through the doors of that institution, they walk in the footsteps of a giant. They are the inheritors of a legacy that is as enduring as the islands themselves—a legacy of hope, of resilience, and of an unwavering belief in the boundless potential of the human spirit.

Major Contributions

  • Clement Howell played a crucial role in the early political and educational development of the Turks and Caicos Islands.
  • As a dedicated educator, he shaped the minds of countless youth in Providenciales, advocating for better resources and an empowering curriculum.
  • In the political arena, he provided vital, stabilizing leadership during a period of deep constitutional crisis as a member of the interim advisory council in 1986, working tirelessly to restore public trust, transparency, and accountability in government.
